rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Avoid aged and matured cheeses, cured or fermented meats and sausages, soy sauce, miso and fermented soybean products, yeast extract (Marmite/Vegemite), and fish sauce.
rules.why: These concentrate tyramine, which your MAOI can no longer break down, so it can push blood pressure up sharply.
rules.source: Van den Eynde V, Gillman PK, Blackwell BB. The Prescriber's Guide to the MAOI Diet — Thinking Through Tyramine Troubles. Psychopharmacol Bull. 2022;52(2):73-116

rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Avoid draught or tap beer and unpasteurised or spontaneously fermented beers such as lambic. Bottled and canned beers are fine in moderation.
rules.why: Draught and spontaneously fermented beers can carry high tyramine from bacterial activity; modern bottled beer measures at or below 2 mg/L.
rules.source: Van den Eynde V, Gillman PK, Blackwell BB. Psychopharmacol Bull. 2022;52(2):73-116 (lambic mean 28 mg/L, max >60 mg/L; bottled beers <=2 mg/L)

rules.label: FOOD
rules.rule: Many foods on the old restriction list are now considered low risk: fresh and commercial cheeses, bottled beer, wine, chocolate, yoghurt, fresh fish and meat, avocado and bananas.
rules.why: Modern production and refrigeration have cut tyramine sharply — most commercial cheeses now measure under 20 mg/kg against historical highs.
rules.source: Van den Eynde V, Gillman PK, Blackwell BB. Psychopharmacol Bull. 2022;52(2):73-116 (brie/camembert <=5 mg/kg modern vs ~100 historical; wine <=5 mg/L; chocolate <10 mg/kg)

rules.label: FOOD
rules.rule: Eat food fresh. Avoid leftovers kept for several days, anything spoiled or past its date, and refrigerate protein foods promptly.
rules.why: Tyramine builds up as protein-rich food ages or sits warm, so a food that is safe when fresh can become risky after storage.
rules.source: Van den Eynde V, Gillman PK, Blackwell BB. Psychopharmacol Bull. 2022;52(2):73-116 (fresh meat <10 mg/kg when stored at or below 4C)

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: Seek urgent care for a sudden severe headache, especially with a pounding or racing heartbeat, chest pain, neck stiffness, nausea or vomiting.
rules.why: These can signal a hypertensive reaction; a sharp systolic rise generally requires more than about 40 mg of tyramine in one meal.
rules.source: Van den Eynde V, Gillman PK, Blackwell BB. Psychopharmacol Bull. 2022;52(2):73-116 (20-30 mg TYR ~30 mmHg systolic rise; >=180 mmHg needs >40 mg)

rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Leave the full washout gap your prescriber sets between an MAOI and another antidepressant — usually 14 days, and about 5 weeks after stopping fluoxetine.
rules.why: MAO enzyme activity takes roughly two weeks to recover, and fluoxetine's long half-life means it lingers in the body for weeks.
rules.source: SSRI/SNRI FDA class labels, Sec 4 Contraindications (14-day MAOI washout); Prozac (fluoxetine) FDA label, Sec 4 (5-week interval)

rules.label: FOOD
rules.rule: Keep your daily salt intake steady. Don't start a low-sodium diet, a sudden high-salt diet, or a major eating change without telling your prescriber first.
rules.why: Your kidneys handle lithium and sodium together, so when sodium drops they hold on to more lithium and your level rises.
rules.source: FDA lithium carbonate label, Sec 5.1 Lithium Toxicity and Sec 5.3 Hyponatremia (DailyMed setid 04518b80-7563-4544-bf05-04f286223faa)

rules.label: HYDRATION
rules.rule: Drink fluids consistently through the day. Labelling points to roughly 2.5 to 3 litres daily, particularly while your dose is still being settled.
rules.why: Steady fluid intake keeps your lithium level stable; falling short concentrates lithium in the blood.
rules.source: FDA lithium carbonate label, Sec 5.3 — 'maintain a normal diet, including salt, and an adequate fluid intake (2,500 to 3,000 mL)'

rules.label: HYDRATION
rules.rule: Take extra care in hot weather, during heavy exercise or sauna use, and when you have vomiting, diarrhoea or fever. Call your prescriber if you can't keep fluids down.
rules.why: Losing body fluid makes the kidneys retain lithium, which can move your level toward the toxic range.
rules.source: FDA lithium carbonate label, Sec 5.1 Lithium Toxicity (volume depletion, dehydration, sodium depletion) and Sec 5.3

rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Check with your prescriber before using ibuprofen, naproxen or other anti-inflammatories. Paracetamol/acetaminophen is usually the safer everyday choice for pain.
rules.why: NSAIDs reduce blood flow through the kidney, which lowers lithium clearance and raises your blood level.
rules.source: FDA lithium carbonate label, Sec 7.1 Drug Interactions — 'NSAID decrease renal blood flow, resulting in decreased renal clearance and increased serum lithium concentrations'

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: Stop lithium and contact your prescriber if you develop diarrhoea, vomiting, tremor, unsteadiness or clumsiness, drowsiness, muscle weakness, or an irregular heartbeat.
rules.why: These are the early signs of lithium toxicity that the label specifically tells patients to act on.
rules.source: FDA lithium carbonate label, Sec 17 Patient Counseling Information (verbatim symptom list)

rules.label: FOOD
rules.rule: Take ziprasidone with a real meal of at least 500 calories, twice a day. Fat content doesn't matter — total calories do. A small snack is not enough.
rules.why: Food roughly doubles absorption; meals around 250 calories give 60-90% lower exposure, so the dose may simply not work.
rules.source: Geodon FDA label Sec 2.1 ('with food') and Sec 7.10 ('absorption increased up to two-fold in the presence of food'; 60% bioavailability fed); Gandelman K, et al. J Clin Psychiatry. 2009;70(1):58-62 (500 kcal threshold)

rules.label: FOOD
rules.rule: Always take vilazodone with food, never on an empty stomach. Pairing it with a regular meal you already eat daily is the easiest way to stay consistent.
rules.why: Fasting cuts absorption by roughly 50% (total exposure) and 60% (peak level), which can leave the dose too low to help.
rules.source: Viibryd (vilazodone) FDA label, Sec 2.1 Dosage and Administration and Sec 12.3 Pharmacokinetics

rules.label: MORNING
rules.rule: Take these in the morning. If you're on a second bupropion dose, space it at least 8 hours after the first and keep it well away from bedtime.
rules.why: Both are activating and can delay sleep; fluoxetine's label specifies morning dosing and lists insomnia at 12-16% versus 7-9% on placebo.
rules.source: Prozac (fluoxetine) FDA label, Sec 2.1 ('in the morning') and Sec 6 Adverse Reactions; Wellbutrin SR/XL FDA label, Sec 2 dosing intervals

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: Some difficulty sleeping in the first few weeks is common. Tell your prescriber if it persists — a timing change often helps — rather than stopping on your own.
rules.why: Activation is a recognised early effect of both drugs and is frequently manageable by adjusting when you take the dose.
rules.source: Insomnia incidence confirmed in Prozac FDA label Sec 6; the claim that it typically settles or resolves with timing changes was NOT confirmed against a primary source

rules.label: EVENING
rules.rule: Take these in the evening, usually at bedtime. If daytime drowsiness is a problem, ask your prescriber about shifting more of the daily dose to bedtime.
rules.why: Both are sedating — mirtazapine mainly through histamine H1 blockade — and drowsiness is reported in roughly 24-41% of people on trazodone.
rules.source: Remeron (mirtazapine) FDA label, Sec 2 (bedtime dosing); trazodone hydrochloride FDA label, Dosage and Administration and Adverse Reactions

rules.label: FOOD
rules.rule: Take trazodone shortly after a meal or a light snack rather than on an empty stomach.
rules.why: Fasting produces a higher and more erratic peak level, which increases dizziness and lightheadedness.
rules.source: Trazodone hydrochloride FDA label, Dosage and Administration ('shortly after a meal or light snack')

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: Don't drive or use machinery until you know how these affect you, and take particular care the morning after starting or increasing a dose.
rules.why: Sedation can carry over into the next day and blunts the alertness and coordination these tasks need.
rules.source: Trazodone hydrochloride FDA label, Warnings and Precautions (impairment of mental/physical ability for hazardous tasks); Remeron FDA label, Sec 5

rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Don't start St John's Wort alongside an antipsychotic such as quetiapine, aripiprazole or lurasidone without telling your prescriber.
rules.why: St John's Wort induces the CYP3A4 enzyme, speeding clearance of these drugs and lowering their blood levels enough to risk relapse.
rules.source: Latuda (lurasidone) FDA label, Sec 4 Contraindications (strong CYP3A4 inducers); StatPearls, St. John's Wort, NCBI Bookshelf NBK557465

rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Don't combine St John's Wort with an SSRI. If you're already taking both, tell your prescriber rather than stopping either one abruptly.
rules.why: Both raise serotonin activity, and the combination has produced serotonin syndrome in published case reports.
rules.source: SSRI class FDA labels, Warnings and Precautions — Serotonin Syndrome (St John's Wort named); StatPearls NBK557465

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: Ask for weight, blood sugar and cholesterol checks before you start and regularly afterwards. Most weight gain happens early, so tracking from day one helps.
rules.why: Olanzapine and clozapine carry the highest metabolic risk of the antipsychotics — clozapine averages about 3 kg more weight gain than placebo.
rules.source: Pillinger T, et al. Lancet Psychiatry. 2020;7(1):64-77; ADA/APA/AACE/NAASO Consensus Development Conference on Antipsychotic Drugs and Obesity and Diabetes. Diabetes Care. 2004;27(2):596-601

rules.label: INFO
rules.rule: This metabolic risk is drug-specific, not true of every antipsychotic. Aripiprazole, lurasidone and ziprasidone have markedly smaller metabolic effects.
rules.why: Network meta-analysis of 100 trials ranks clozapine and olanzapine worst, and aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine, lurasidone and ziprasidone most benign.
rules.source: Pillinger T, et al. Comparative effects of 18 antipsychotics on metabolic function. Lancet Psychiatry. 2020;7(1):64-77

rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Keep alcohol low and steady, and don't stop drinking abruptly if you drink regularly. Talk to your prescriber before changing your intake either way.
rules.why: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and abrupt alcohol withdrawal lowers it further; the label contraindicates that combination.
rules.source: Wellbutrin XL (bupropion) FDA label, Sec 4 Contraindications (abrupt discontinuation of alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, antiepileptics) and Sec 5.3 Seizure

rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Bupropion isn't suitable if you have or have had bulimia or anorexia nervosa. Tell your prescriber about any eating disorder history, including past episodes.
rules.why: A higher rate of seizures was seen in patients with these diagnoses, so the label lists them as contraindications.
rules.source: Wellbutrin XL (bupropion) FDA label, Sec 4 Contraindications

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: Take bupropion exactly as prescribed and never double up after a missed dose. Swallow extended-release tablets whole rather than crushing or splitting them.
rules.why: Seizure risk is dose-related — about 0.4% at 300-450 mg/day immediate-release — and rises sharply with higher doses or sudden peak levels.
rules.source: Wellbutrin FDA label, Sec 5.3 Seizure and Sec 2 Dosage and Administration

rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Alcohol is best avoided or kept low, especially in the early weeks. It deepens drowsiness and low mood and makes it harder to tell how the medicine is working.
rules.why: SSRI labels advise avoiding alcohol; sedation is additive and alcohol independently worsens depressive symptoms and sleep quality.
rules.source: SSRI/SNRI class FDA labels, Sec 17 Patient Counseling Information — alcohol

rules.label: FOOD
rules.rule: Nausea, loose stools or general stomach upset are common in the first weeks. Taking your dose with food often makes this easier.
rules.why: Most of the body's serotonin receptors sit in the gut, so raising serotonin commonly unsettles digestion at first.
rules.source: Nausea is documented as the most common adverse reaction in SSRI/SNRI FDA labels Sec 6; the timeframe ('first weeks', 'usually eases') and the food-mitigation tip were NOT confirmed against a primary source

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: Don't stop an antidepressant suddenly. Ask your prescriber for a taper plan, even if you're feeling well or want to come off quickly.
rules.why: Stopping abruptly can bring dizziness, flu-like feelings, irritability, vivid dreams and brief electric-shock sensations while the brain readjusts.
rules.source: Warner CH, Bobo W, Warner C, Reid S, Rachal J. Antidepressant Discontinuation Syndrome. Am Fam Physician. 2006;74(3):449-456

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: These need an especially slow, planned taper, and a missed dose is felt quickly. Keep a steady schedule and don't let your supply run out.
rules.why: Their short half-lives mean blood levels drop fast, and they carry the highest reported rates of discontinuation symptoms.
rules.source: Warner CH, et al. Am Fam Physician. 2006;74(3):449-456; comparative WHO VigiBase pharmacovigilance analysis of withdrawal syndrome across 15 antidepressants, J Affect Disord. 2022

rules.label: INFO
rules.rule: Fluoxetine is generally the easiest antidepressant to come off, and a missed dose is less noticeable. It still deserves a planned taper, just usually a simpler one.
rules.why: Its long half-life and long-lasting active metabolite mean levels fall gradually, so it partly self-tapers; it has the lowest reported discontinuation rates.
rules.source: Warner CH, et al. Am Fam Physician. 2006;74(3):449-456

rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Check before regular use of ibuprofen, naproxen or aspirin. Occasional use is usually fine — ask sooner if you're on a blood thinner or have had a stomach ulcer.
rules.why: These antidepressants reduce platelet serotonin and impair clotting; combined with NSAIDs the risk of upper gut bleeding rises several-fold.
rules.source: SSRI/SNRI FDA labels, Warnings and Precautions — Abnormal Bleeding (FDA-required class labeling extended to duloxetine and venlafaxine)

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: Mention easy bruising, nosebleeds that are slow to stop, or black or tarry stools to your prescriber.
rules.why: These can be early signs of the platelet effect; black stools in particular may point to bleeding in the upper gut.
rules.source: SSRI/SNRI FDA labels, Warnings and Precautions — Abnormal Bleeding

rules.label: AVOID
rules.rule: Never take an antidepressant together with an MAOI, and tell any prescriber you're on one before you start linezolid or receive methylene blue.
rules.why: These block serotonin breakdown while the antidepressant raises serotonin — the combination most strongly linked to serotonin syndrome.
rules.source: SSRI/SNRI FDA labels, Sec 4 Contraindications and Sec 5 Warnings — Serotonin Syndrome; FDA Drug Safety Communication (2011): linezolid and methylene blue with serotonergic psychiatric medications

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: Tell your prescriber before starting tramadol or fentanyl. If you do need them, watch closely for agitation, sweating, shivering or muscle twitching.
rules.why: Both add serotonin activity, and among opioids they show the strongest serotonin syndrome signal in pharmacovigilance data.
rules.source: FDA Drug Safety Communication (2016): opioids combined with serotonergic drugs; FAERS disproportionality analysis, Med Princ Pract. 2025;34(5):456

rules.label: INFO
rules.rule: Triptans for migraine can usually be used alongside an SSRI or SNRI. Mention the combination to your prescriber, but it rarely causes problems in practice.
rules.why: FDA issued an alert in 2006, but later review found the real-world risk very low — worth knowing about rather than avoiding.
rules.source: FDA Alert (2006): triptans with SSRIs/SNRIs; American Headache Society position paper on serotonin syndrome with triptans, Headache. 2010;50(6):1089-1099

rules.label: WATCH
rules.rule: Get urgent help for agitation or confusion combined with fever, heavy sweating, shivering, a fast heartbeat, or muscle twitching or stiffness.
rules.why: That cluster suggests serotonin syndrome, which is most likely soon after starting a serotonergic drug, raising a dose, or adding a second one.
rules.source: SSRI/SNRI FDA labels, Warnings and Precautions — Serotonin Syndrome (symptom cluster verbatim)

notes:
SOURCING METHOD AND CONFIDENCE

Three sources were fetched and read directly in full, so quotes from them are verbatim and high confidence:
1. Van den Eynde V, Gillman PK, Blackwell BB. "The Prescriber's Guide to the MAOI Diet — Thinking Through Tyramine Troubles." Psychopharmacology Bulletin. 2022;52(2):73-116. PMC9172554. This is the modern authority on narrowing the tyramine list and supplied both the avoid-list and the reclassified-as-low-risk list with measured tyramine concentrations.
2. FDA lithium carbonate label via DailyMed (setid 04518b80-7563-4544-bf05-04f286223faa) — Sec 5.1, 5.3, 7.1 and 17 quoted directly, including the "2,500 to 3,000 mL" fluid figure and the verbatim toxicity symptom list.
3. FDA ziprasidone label via DailyMed (setid 7fbd9460-78a3-4160-9986-3a113de752a6) — Sec 7.10 Food Interaction, confirming "absorption is increased up to two-fold in the presence of food" and 60% absolute bioavailability fed.

The remaining citations were confirmed through search-result extracts of primary documents (accessdata.fda.gov label PDFs, PubMed/PMC abstracts) rather than by fetching each document end to end. Several accessdata.fda.gov PDF URLs returned HTTP 404 to the fetch tool during this pass (Lithobid 018027s064, Wellbutrin XL 021515s046, Viibryd 022567s025, Prozac 202133s004, Remeron 020415s038). The underlying facts were corroborated from search extracts of those same documents, but before production use each of these should be re-verified against the current label PDF, and the label section numbers I cite should be re-checked since section numbering shifts between label revisions.

IMPORTANT ACCURACY FLAGS

ZIPRASIDONE 500 CALORIES IS NOT AN FDA LABEL FIGURE. This is the single most likely thing to be mis-attributed downstream. The FDA label says only "with food" (Sec 2.1) and quantifies the two-fold absorption effect (Sec 7.10). The specific 500-kcal threshold comes from Gandelman K, et al. J Clin Psychiatry. 2009;70(1):58-62, which found 250-kcal meals gave 60-90% lower exposure than 500- and 1000-kcal meals, and that fat content had no significant effect. The rule cites both sources separately for this reason. Do not render this as "the FDA says 500 calories."

ST JOHN'S WORT AND ANTIPSYCHOTICS IS DRUG-SPECIFIC BY ENZYME. CYP3A4 induction meaningfully lowers levels of quetiapine, aripiprazole and lurasidone. It is much less relevant to clozapine and olanzapine, which are cleared mainly via CYP1A2 — for those two, smoking status is the far larger driver of level changes. I did not verify a CYP1A2/smoking rule in this pass, so it is not included; it is a real gap worth filling. I also could not fetch the Latuda label directly to confirm St John's Wort is named by name in its contraindications (as opposed to "strong CYP3A4 inducers" generically) — worth a targeted check.

TRIPTAN RISK IS DELIBERATELY DOWNGRADED TO INFO. The 2006 FDA alert is real, but subsequent review (American Headache Society position paper, Headache 2010) found the actual incidence very low. Flagging this as critical would push patients away from effective migraine treatment for little safety gain. The genuinely high-signal serotonin syndrome combinations are MAOIs, linezolid, methylene blue, and the high-risk opioids tramadol and fentanyl — those are marked critical/caution accordingly.

METABOLIC RISK IS DRUG-SPECIFIC, NOT CLASS-WIDE. Two separate rules encode this deliberately, because collapsing it into "antipsychotics cause weight gain" is both inaccurate and clinically harmful — it discourages patients on aripiprazole, lurasidone or ziprasidone unnecessarily. Pillinger 2020 (Lancet Psychiatry, 100 trials, 25,952 patients) is the cleanest comparative source.

DISCONTINUATION NUANCE IS SPLIT ACROSS THREE RULES rather than one, because paroxetine/venlafaxine/desvenlafaxine, the general SSRI case, and fluoxetine genuinely differ. Note that fluoxetine's mildness is a double-edged fact clinically: it is also why fluoxetine is used as a bridging agent when tapering off a short-half-life agent. That bridging strategy is a prescriber decision, not patient lifestyle advice, so it is not encoded as a rule.

TWO RULES ARE MARKED verified=false

1. Fluoxetine/bupropion insomnia "often settles / timing change helps." The insomnia incidence figures are solidly from the Prozac label (12-16% vs 7-9% placebo in MDD). The reassurance that it typically resolves, and that re-timing fixes it, is widely-held clinical practice but I did not locate a primary source quantifying it. Either source it or soften the wording before shipping.

2. SSRI GI upset "common in the first weeks, usually eases, food helps." Nausea being the most common SSRI adverse reaction is well documented in the labels. The specific time course and the take-with-food mitigation are clinical convention, not label statements. This one matters less for safety but should not carry an implied citation.

TONE NOTE

Rules are written to be actionable without alarming — "check with your prescriber before" rather than "never take," reassurance rules included alongside restriction rules (particularly the MAOI low-risk-foods rule, which exists specifically to counter the outdated and needlessly frightening restriction lists patients still encounter online). The MAOI, lithium and bupropion critical rules are the ones where firm language is warranted and is used.

COVERAGE GAPS NOT ADDRESSED

Smoking and CYP1A2 (affects clozapine and olanzapine levels substantially, including on quitting); caffeine interaction with lithium and clozapine; grapefruit juice and CYP3A4 substrates; lamotrigine rash and titration; MAOI interactions with sympathomimetics and decongestants (pseudoephedrine), which are arguably as important as the tyramine diet and are a notable omission from the requested scope; QT prolongation for citalopram and ziprasidone. Each of these is a legitimate lifestyle-protocol entry and would need its own sourcing pass.
